title: Swadeshi: more than a slogan
author: Editorial Desk
summary: What Thengadi meant when he spoke of self-reliance, and why it appears in BMS demands.
body:
Dattopant Thengadi was a leading figure behind the **Swadeshi Jagaran Manch (SJM)**, which was founded on 22 November 1991 in Nagpur, at the time when India opened its economy to liberalisation. Its first convener was Dr M. G. Bokare, an economist and former Vice-Chancellor of Nagpur University. The Manch took the view that opening up must be done on India's terms and with safeguards for domestic producers and workers. This post explains the circumstances of 1991, what swadeshi means as BMS uses the word, how it connects to labour demands, and why the idea needs to be tested by results and not just repeated.

## The year 1991

To understand why swadeshi became an organised cause in 1991, one has to recall the crisis of that year. India's foreign exchange reserves were about 1.2 billion US dollars in January 1991, and they fell by half by June, enough for only about three weeks of essential imports. The Government secured an emergency IMF loan and pledged gold as collateral. The rupee was devalued by 9 per cent on 1 July and by 11 per cent on 3 July. P. V. Narasimha Rao had become Prime Minister in June and appointed Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, and the budget speech of 24 July 1991 set out a reform programme that included deregulation of industry, reduced import licensing, foreign equity of up to 51 per cent in high-priority industries and a limited disinvestment of public sector undertakings.

These steps opened the economy. Many saw them as necessary, and others feared for domestic industry and jobs. BMS was among the organisations that voiced concern. According to a reference history of the union, it opposed conditions of the IMF and the World Bank as an infringement of national sovereignty and called the New Economic Policy a second war of economic independence. The Swadeshi Jagaran Manch was formed in that debate as a platform for the view that India should open its economy on its own terms.

## What swadeshi means

The dbthengadi.in archive lists talks by Thengadi on the concept of swadeshi, economic imperialism and the World Trade Organization, which shows how central the idea was to his economic thinking. Swadeshi does not mean isolation. In the way BMS presents it, it means:

- **Priority to the local producer** where quality and price are comparable.
- **Fair terms in trade agreements**, so that Indian industry and workers are not exposed to unfair competition.
- **Technology on our terms:** acquiring foreign technology, but not becoming dependent on it.
- **Self-reliance** in strategic areas such as defence, energy and health.

The Manch describes itself as an economic and cultural organisation that promotes national self-reliance, and its work consists of conferences, seminars, study circles, publications and training programmes on entrepreneurship, manufacturing, technology and agriculture. It has taken public positions on economic policy, including criticism of foreign direct investment since at least 2015 and, in 2018, opposition to FDI in single-brand retail and to foreign investment in Air India.

## Connection to labour

The link between swadeshi and labour is practical. BMS calls for protection of **micro, small and medium enterprises**, which employ crores of people, and opposes the disinvestment of public sector undertakings that work in the national interest. On 10 June 2020 it called a nationwide movement against the privatisation of public-sector undertakings. The union's motto, "Industrialise the Nation! Labourise the Industry! Nationalise the Labour!", expresses the same thought: industrial growth must be built around the worker.

The MSME sector is the best illustration. According to the Ministry of MSME's year-end review for 2025, over 7.30 crore enterprises were registered on the Udyam portal by December 2025, the sector supports the livelihoods of over 12 crore people, contributes around 30 per cent of GDP and 36 per cent of manufacturing output, and accounts for nearly 45 per cent of India's exports. These are the units that a swadeshi policy is expected to protect: small, local and dependent on a fair market. BMS argues that an economy with strong domestic industry has more secure jobs.

## Against speculation

Another strand in Thengadi's thought, as recorded by an admirer's tribute, was a dislike of speculation in the stock exchange, derivatives and forward trading, which, the tribute says, he believed cause artificial price rises and scarcity. Whether or not one agrees, the point shows the consistency of the thought: money should serve production, and production should serve people.

## A caution against slogans

Swadeshi, like any idea, can become a slogan. A policy is not swadeshi simply because it carries the label, nor is it un-swadeshi merely because it involves a foreign partner. The test is practical:

- Does a policy create **jobs here**?
- Does it respect the **worker**, with a wage, a contract and social security?
- Does it build **capability** in Indian firms, or only a temporary advantage?
- Is it open to **review** if it does not deliver?

These tests cut both ways. They apply to a protective duty, a subsidy and a trade agreement alike. They also apply to a plan for opening an industry to foreign investment, which should be judged by what happens to Indian producers and workers.

## Why the debate continues

It is easy to treat liberalisation and swadeshi as opposites, but the record is more mixed. The 1991 crisis was real, and the reforms that followed responded to it. The concerns of those who asked for safeguards were also real, since a small producer does not have the resources of a multinational. The useful question for a trade union is not whether to be for or against openness, but on what terms, with what protection for the worker who loses a job when a factory closes and with what training for the one who gets a new one.

## What remains

The questions swadeshi raises have not gone away. India's trade agreements, its technology choices, the survival of small units and the role of public enterprises are live questions. For workers, the point is that employment is not an automatic by-product of growth; it depends on the choices that a country makes about what to make, who makes it and on what terms. A debate on those choices that includes the voice of labour is part of what BMS means when it speaks of the nation and the worker together.
